p: Ohio's withholding formula changes effective August 1, 2026, and the calculator above applies whichever version matches the period being modelled. On a biweekly schedule the switch falls inside a pay cycle rather than between two of them.

That means 2026 Ohio withholding is not one rate applied 26 times. Roughly the first fifteen checks use the old formula and the rest use the new one, so a full-year figure projected from a single spring paycheck will be wrong in a predictable direction.

sections.h2: Municipal tax and school district tax can both ride on the same Ohio paycheck
p: Ohio has more local income taxing jurisdictions than any other state. A municipal income tax follows the worksite, a school district income tax follows your residence, and it is entirely possible to have both withheld from the same biweekly check alongside the state line.

The calculator above takes municipal and school district rates as separate entries because no statewide figure exists. For many Ohio workers the combined local deduction is larger than the state one, which is why estimating an Ohio paycheck from the state rate alone is close to useless.

sections.h2: Ohio has reciprocity with five states, but only for the state line
p: Ohio maintains reciprocal agreements with Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Pennsylvania and West Virginia. Residents of those states working in Ohio file Form IT-4NR and have no Ohio state income tax withheld.

Municipal taxes are outside every one of those agreements. A Pennsylvania resident working in Cincinnati can have zero Ohio state withholding and a full Cincinnati municipal deduction on all 26 checks. Reciprocity stops the state line and nothing else.

sections.h2: Oklahoma rounds every biweekly paycheck to a whole dollar
p: Oklahoma's percentage method computes the tax for the pay period and rounds it to whole dollars, which the calculator above reproduces. Across 26 periods those roundings accumulate into an annual figure slightly different from an exact calculation.
This is why the Oklahoma line on your stub never shows cents, and why the same salary paid semi-monthly produces a marginally different annual total. It is the method, not a payroll error.

sections.h2: Oklahoma's top bracket starts low, so most workers sit in it
p: Oklahoma's graduated brackets compress quickly — the top rate begins at a taxable income level that most full-time workers exceed. In effect Oklahoma behaves like a flat-rate state for the majority of biweekly earners.

The practical consequence is that a raise rarely produces a bracket jump in the state line the way it can in Minnesota or New York. The Oklahoma state percentage on paycheck 26 is usually close to what it was on paycheck 1.

sections.h2: Oklahoma has no reciprocity, and it borders six states
p: Oklahoma maintains no reciprocal agreements. Texas takes nothing, so that direction is straightforward. Kansas, Missouri, Arkansas, Colorado and New Mexico all tax income earned within their borders and will withhold from an Oklahoma resident working there.

Arkansas is the one to watch, because it applies a convenience-of-the-employer rule: remote work for an Arkansas employer can be sourced to Arkansas even when performed in Oklahoma, producing Arkansas withholding on all 26 checks.

sections.h2: Oregon's Workers' Benefit Fund is charged by the hour, so your schedule changes it
p: Oregon's Workers' Benefit Fund assessment is a cents-per-hour charge on hours worked, not a percentage of wages. The calculator above takes the employee rate in cents and your annual hours. That makes it the one deduction on this page that depends on how many hours a pay period contains rather than how much it pays.

Two Oregon employees on identical salaries with different schedules — one full-time salaried, one working longer hours — pay different WBF amounts. It is also the reason an Oregon estimate needs an hours figure at all, which no other state on this site requires.

sections.h2: Oregon stacks transit tax and Paid Leave on top of income tax
p: Oregon withholds a statewide transit tax of 0.1% of wages, an employee Paid Leave premium on wages up to $184,500, and the WBF hourly assessment, all alongside income tax. The transit tax is computed per pay period and truncated to the cent, so it is 26 small identical deductions.

The Paid Leave premium stops once you cross the wage base, the transit tax never stops, and the WBF depends on hours. Three different behaviours on the same stub is unusual, and it is why an Oregon paycheck is one of the harder ones to reproduce from a single rate.

sections.h2: With no Oregon withholding form on file, the fallback is 8% of everything
p: Oregon's default for an employee with no state withholding certificate is a flat 8% of wages, which the calculator above applies when you indicate no form is on file. For most earners that is well above the correct rate.

Applied across 26 biweekly checks, the excess is substantial and does not come back until filing. Oregon also has no sales tax, which is the trade-off for a relatively heavy income tax — but the 8% fallback is not a trade-off, it is just a missing form.

sections.h2: Pennsylvania's 3.07% applies from the first dollar with no standard deduction
p: Pennsylvania levies a flat 3.07% on compensation with no standard deduction, no personal exemption and no allowances. The calculator above applies it directly to wages. That makes the state line the most predictable item on a Pennsylvania stub: 3.07% of gross, all 26 periods, at every salary.

It also means Pennsylvania takes more from low earners as a share of income than almost any bracketed state, and less from high earners. There is no form to tune and nothing to claim — the only Pennsylvania variable is the local rate.

sections.h2: The local EIT is a separate tax with its own rate and its own rules
p: Pennsylvania municipalities and school districts levy an Earned Income Tax, withheld from each biweekly paycheck on top of the state's 3.07%. The combined local rate varies widely, and Philadelphia runs its own separate wage tax at a substantially higher rate than most of the commonwealth.

The calculator above takes the local rate as an entry. Pennsylvania's rule is generally that you pay the higher of your resident or worksite rate, with the revenue split between jurisdictions — so moving house can change your withholding even if your job does not.

sections.h2: Pennsylvania has reciprocity with six states and a convenience rule of its own
p: Pennsylvania maintains reciprocal agreements with Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, Ohio, Virginia and West Virginia. Residents of those states working in Pennsylvania file Form REV-419 and have no Pennsylvania state withholding.

New York is not a partner, and Pennsylvania applies its own convenience-of-the-employer rule to remote workers on Pennsylvania payrolls. The agreements also cover the state line only — the local EIT and the Philadelphia wage tax are outside them, so a New Jersey resident working in Philadelphia can have no Pennsylvania state tax and a full city wage tax on all 26 checks.

sections.h2: Rhode Island withholds Temporary Disability Insurance from the employee
p: Rhode Island is one of the few states with an employee-funded Temporary Disability Insurance programme. The TDI contribution is withheld from wages up to an annual taxable wage base, so for higher earners it stops partway through the year and the remaining biweekly deposits are larger.
The table above models income tax. The TDI line is separate, and it is the main reason a Rhode Island stub carries a state deduction that a Connecticut or Massachusetts stub structures differently.

sections.h2: Rhode Island exemptions phase out at higher incomes
p: Rhode Island's personal exemption, claimed on the state RI W-4, is reduced and eventually eliminated above an income threshold. The calculator above applies the exemption value you enter.

On a biweekly schedule the effect is that the same number of exemptions is worth progressively less as salary rises, and worth nothing at all above the phase-out. Someone comparing their state line against a lower-paid colleague's will find the difference larger than the salary gap alone explains.

sections.h2: Rhode Island has no reciprocity with Massachusetts or Connecticut
p: Rhode Island maintains no reciprocal agreements. Both of its neighbours tax income earned within their borders, and Rhode Island is small enough that a large share of its workforce crosses a state line to work.

A Rhode Island resident working in Massachusetts has Massachusetts tax withheld from all 26 checks and claims a Rhode Island credit at filing. Connecticut's retaliatory convenience provision can also reach a Rhode Island resident working remotely for a Connecticut employer.

sections.h2: South Carolina's brackets compress to a single effective rate quickly
p: South Carolina has collapsed its bracket structure so that most of the range is taxed at the top rate, with a large zero-rate band at the bottom. The WH-1603F annualized formula in the calculator above reflects that shape.

For a biweekly earner the result is a state line that stays at zero or near-zero at low salaries and then rises quickly to a near-constant percentage. The steep part of that curve is narrow, so two colleagues a few thousand dollars apart in salary can have noticeably different effective state rates.

sections.h2: South Carolina's rate has been stepping down annually
p: South Carolina has been reducing its top marginal rate on a legislated schedule, contingent on revenue targets being met. The calculator above uses the current year's rate.

That makes year-over-year stub comparison misleading: an identical salary yields a smaller state line each year the reduction proceeds. It also means a full-year projection built from a January paycheck can be slightly off if the schedule advances.

sections.h2: South Carolina has no reciprocity, and Charlotte straddles the border
p: South Carolina maintains no reciprocal agreements with North Carolina or Georgia. Both tax income earned within their borders, so a South Carolina resident working across either line has two states withholding from the same 26 checks.

The Charlotte metropolitan area is the busiest version of this — a large number of South Carolina residents work at North Carolina worksites. North Carolina withholds on the work performed there and South Carolina gives a credit at filing, a year after the money left the paycheck.

sections.h2: Utah's withholding tables change on June 1, 2026, splitting the biweekly year
p: Utah's Publication 14 tables change effective June 1, 2026, and the calculator above applies whichever version matches the pay period. On a 26-period schedule that date falls inside a pay cycle rather than between two of them.

So 2026 Utah withholding is roughly the first eleven checks on one table and the rest on another. Projecting a full year from a single spring paycheck will be wrong, and the direction of the error depends on which way the tables moved.

sections.h2: Utah gives a credit that phases out, not an allowance
p: Utah applies a single rate to all taxable income and then subtracts a taxpayer credit that phases out as income rises. The calculator above computes the period tax, subtracts the credit and rounds.

The practical effect is a state line that behaves progressively even though the rate is flat. At lower salaries the credit cancels much of the tax; at higher ones it is gone entirely. Reading Utah's flat rate as your effective rate will overstate withholding at the bottom of the range and match it at the top.

sections.h2: Utah has no reciprocity, and four neighbours tax income
p: Utah maintains no reciprocal agreements. Nevada and Wyoming levy no income tax, so work performed there creates no second state line. Idaho, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico all tax income earned within their borders and will withhold from a Utah resident working there.

Arizona is the partial exception in the other direction: Arizona's reciprocity list includes California, Indiana, Oregon and Virginia, not Utah, so a Utah resident working in Arizona is withheld by Arizona and credited by Utah at filing.

sections.h2: Vermont allowances come from Form W-4VT, not the federal W-4
p: Vermont's GB-1210 method uses allowances claimed on Form W-4VT. Since the federal W-4 dropped allowances, Vermont employees who never completed the state form are commonly withheld at a default that does not match their situation.

That default applies to all 26 biweekly checks before anything reconciles. If the Vermont line on your stub runs above the figures in the table, the missing W-4VT is the first thing to check — it is the single most common cause.

sections.h2: Vermont's top bracket is high relative to the size of the state's brackets
p: Vermont runs graduated brackets with a comparatively high top rate, and withholding is computed by annualizing the biweekly wage. Crossing a bracket therefore changes the state line on every remaining paycheck of the year, not just the one where the raise landed.
It also makes irregular periods conspicuous. A biweekly check containing a bonus is annualized as though the bonus repeated 26 times, so that period is over-withheld and the excess returns at filing.

sections.h2: Vermont has no reciprocity, and New Hampshire next door taxes nothing
p: Vermont maintains no reciprocal agreements. New Hampshire has no wage income tax, so a Vermont resident working across that border has only Vermont in their withholding — but a New Hampshire resident working in Vermont has Vermont tax withheld from all 26 checks with no home-state credit to claim.

Massachusetts and New York, the other two neighbours, both tax income earned within their borders, and New York's convenience rule can reach a Vermont resident working remotely for a New York employer.

sections.h2: Virginia's withholding formula changed in July 2025 and has not changed since
p: The calculator above uses Virginia's withholding formula effective July 2025 and later. If you are comparing against a stub from the first half of 2025, the method differs — that mid-year change split the biweekly year the way Georgia's, Ohio's and Utah's do in 2026.

For 2026 the formula is stable across all 26 periods, which makes Virginia easier to project than several of its neighbours. A January paycheck is a reliable guide to a December one at the same salary.

sections.h2: Virginia's brackets have not been indexed, so the top one starts very low
p: Virginia's top bracket begins at a taxable income level set decades ago and never adjusted for inflation. Almost every full-time worker is in it, which means Virginia behaves like a flat-rate state in practice despite having four brackets on paper.

For a biweekly earner this makes the state line highly predictable: a near-constant percentage of gross across all 26 checks, with little bracket effect from a raise. The exemptions claimed on Form VA-4 are the main lever, and Virginia also provides additional exemptions for age and blindness.

sections.h2: Virginia has reciprocity with five jurisdictions
p: Virginia maintains reciprocal agreements with the District of Columbia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, West Virginia and Kentucky. Residents of those places working in Virginia file Form VA-4 and have no Virginia withholding.

This is what makes the Washington metropolitan area workable: a Virginia resident working in DC or Maryland has one jurisdiction in their withholding rather than two. North Carolina and Tennessee are not partners — Tennessee takes nothing, but a North Carolina worksite means withholding from both states on all 26 checks.

sections.h2: Washington has no income tax but two payroll programmes that hit every check
p: Washington does not tax wages, yet a Washington stub is not blank in the state column. The employee share of Paid Family and Medical Leave applies to wages up to $184,500, and the WA Cares long-term care premium applies at 0.58% with no wage ceiling at all.

The table above now shows these under State Payroll. It is why a Washington biweekly deposit is smaller than an otherwise identical Texas or Florida deposit at the same salary, despite both states being described as having no income tax.

sections.h2: The two Washington programmes stop at different points, or not at all
p: Paid Leave stops once your wages cross $184,500, on the same paycheck Social Security stops. WA Cares has no ceiling, so it continues on all 26 checks at every salary.

For a high earner that produces a distinctive late-year pattern: one paycheck where two deductions disappear together and one small deduction carries on. Below the base both run all year, and the combined effect is a little over 1% of gross.

sections.h2: Washington has no income tax to credit, so an Oregon commute is expensive
p: A Washington resident working in Oregon has Oregon income tax withheld from all 26 biweekly checks, plus Oregon's transit tax and Paid Leave premium on the work performed there. Washington offers no credit, because it has no income tax against which one could be applied.

That asymmetry is the defining fact of the Portland–Vancouver labour market. Running the other way, an Oregon resident working in Washington pays Oregon on the income anyway, since Oregon taxes its residents on all income regardless of source.

sections.h2: Wisconsin's W-166 method annualizes and rounds each biweekly period
p: Wisconsin's W-166 annualized method computes the tax from annualized wages, then rounds at the pay-period level before dividing across 26 checks. The calculator above follows that sequence.

As with the other per-period rounding states, this means 26 rounded periods do not sum to an exact annual figure, and the same salary paid on a different frequency produces a slightly different annual total.

sections.h2: The WT-4 lets you add or subtract a fixed amount from every check
p: Wisconsin's Form WT-4 carries both an additional-withholding line and a reduced-withholding line, and the calculator above accepts both. Few states allow employees to formally request less withholding than the tables produce.

On a biweekly schedule each entry is a flat per-check adjustment applied 26 times, so a $10 line is $260 over the year. The reduction option is genuinely useful for employees whose tables over-withhold, but it puts the burden of getting it right on you rather than on the formula.

sections.h2: Wisconsin has reciprocity with four states, but not Minnesota
p: Wisconsin maintains reciprocal agreements with Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky and Michigan. Residents of those states working in Wisconsin file Form W-220 and have no Wisconsin withholding.

Minnesota is the conspicuous absence. The Wisconsin–Minnesota agreement ended years ago, so a Wisconsin resident working in Minneapolis has Minnesota tax withheld from all 26 checks and claims a Wisconsin credit at filing. For the Twin Cities and La Crosse commuter belts this is the single most consequential payroll fact in the state.

sections.h2: West Virginia runs two different tables depending on household earners
p: West Virginia's IT-100.2A method uses a one-earner table and a two-earner table, and the calculator above applies whichever matches your situation. Most states handle this through a filing status; West Virginia handles it through an entirely separate rate schedule.

Selecting the wrong one on Form IT-104 misstates withholding on all 26 biweekly checks. The two-earner table withholds more at the same wage, because it assumes household income that the single wage alone does not reveal.

sections.h2: West Virginia's rate has been stepping down under a trigger mechanism
p: West Virginia has legislated reductions in its income tax rates tied to revenue triggers, so the rate can fall in some years and hold in others. The calculator above uses the current schedule.

Because the reductions are conditional rather than fixed, a multi-year projection built from today's biweekly figure is less reliable in West Virginia than in states on a fixed step-down. Check the current rate each January rather than assuming last year's stub still applies.

sections.h2: West Virginia has reciprocity with five neighbours
p: West Virginia maintains reciprocal agreements with Kentucky, Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Virginia — every state it borders. Residents of those states working in West Virginia file Form WV/IT-104R and have no West Virginia withholding, and West Virginia residents working there are taxed at home instead.

That full coverage is unusual and it makes West Virginia one of the simplest states in the country for cross-border payroll. The exception is local tax: Ohio municipal taxes and Pennsylvania's local EIT sit outside the agreements and can still be withheld from a West Virginia resident's paycheck.
